queue.recognise: You can recognise it as the giant redwood standing in the open at the southern end of Redford Wood, north-west of Dreghorn Barracks; the wood's other redwoods stand among the trees.
queue.story:
A prince of Siam is said to have planted this giant sequoia when he finished his military training at the barracks next to Redford Wood. That is how the City of Edinburgh Council told it on its heritage tree list, around 2012, putting the planting at approximately a hundred years before. A walker's account from 2017 gives the year as 1909. Neither cites a document, so treat the prince and the date as the story the tree carries rather than a record, and the age as somewhere around 100 to 120 years.

It is not alone. Redford Wood holds several giant redwoods of similar girth, along with veteran oak, beech, lime, ash, sycamore and yew. The council picked this one out as a particularly fine spec
queue.name: The Redford Wood Redwood

queue.tree_name: Giant Australian Rubber Tree of Jardim Antonio Borges
queue.recognise: You can recognise it by the mass of aerial roots and its botanical label. It stands in the south-east part of the garden, along the Central Alley.
queue.story:
In the Azores this is an Australian rubber tree. Botanists know it as a Moreton Bay Fig, and the regional government's own sheet on the Jardim António Borges simply calls it colossal. That sheet, from the Azorean environment directorate, singles it out for its fantastic aerial roots and counts it among the largest and oldest trees on the garden's botanical route.

The fig grows in the south-east part of the garden, along the Central Alley, and carries a botanical label, so it is not hard to find. Its roots are the point. A Moreton Bay Fig lets them down from its branches. Nobody has published its girth or height, so the word colossal is the only measurement on record.

queue.recognise: You can recognise it as the broad old yew just over the wall from Colinton Parish Church's churchyard, about 3.5 metres round. It stands in the manse garden, and one limb still carries what is left of Stevenson's swing.
queue.story:
The remains of Robert Louis Stevenson's childhood swing still hang from a limb of this yew, according to the City of Edinburgh Council. Stevenson spent much of his boyhood at Colinton Manse, played in the tree, and later put it into A Child's Garden of Verses, the book of poems about being small that he wrote as a grown man, in the same years he was writing Treasure Island and Kidnapped.

The council puts the yew at 300 to 400 years old and names it among Scotland's top 100 heritage trees. Yews keep their age to themselves, so take that as an estimate rather than a birth date.
